---
title: "Read Your Writes Across Two Regions"
description: "Challenging system-design interview scenario: formal guarantee, failures, and an original implementation."
---

## Interview challenge

A user updates their profile in Region A and is immediately routed to Region B for the next GET request. Region B asynchronously replicates data and currently holds the old version. The user reports that their newly saved settings have disappeared.

How do we guarantee **read-your-writes** without making every read globally synchronous?

## Specify the guarantee first

A client that committed version $v$ should not be served a version older than $v$ on a later read in the same session:

$$
v_{\mathrm{read}}\geq v_{\mathrm{lastCommittedByClient}}.
$$

This is **session consistency**, not automatically global linearizability. Other clients may observe a different freshness level under asynchronous replication.

## One small mechanism

Return a version token after each successful write. Carry the highest seen version on subsequent reads. A replica may serve a request only when its local version is sufficient. Otherwise it can wait for replication until the caller's deadline, route the read to the leader/origin region, or return an explicit retryable status.

~~~ts
const clientRequires = 12;
const replica = { version: 11, value: 'old' };
if (replica.version < clientRequires) {
  // Do not return this replica's stale value as a successful session read.
}
~~~

The shared [VersionedCache](../lab/src/core.ts) illustrates monotonic version writes, but the educational lab **does not implement cross-region replication or a session protocol**.

## Why the simple 'always read nearest' answer fails

After a successful write, routing the next request to any available nearest replica breaks read-your-writes if that replica lags. Sticky routing reduces the chance but cannot guarantee the property after failover.

A global strongly consistent read would solve the issue but can increase latency and reduce availability under partitions. Session tokens offer a narrower and often cheaper guarantee.

## The genuinely difficult edge case

What if version 12 was committed only in Region A, but A becomes unreachable and B has only version 11? You cannot simultaneously promise an immediately available read from B and strict read-your-writes from the missing version. Choose to wait, fail, or weaken the guarantee and **tell the client**.

Likewise, independent writes in both regions may require conflict resolution (leader assignment, version vectors, CRDT semantics or business-specific merges). A simple scalar version from one leader does not solve concurrent multi-leader writes.

## Interview follow-ups

- Can you use client-side local state to display an optimistic profile? Yes, but distinguish UI presentation from an authoritative persisted read.
- How do you bound waiting? Propagate a deadline. Exceeding it returns a clear timeout/unavailable response, not silently stale data.
- Should every service use global linearizability? No; design per business invariant.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
\operatorname{read}(k,\mathrm{session}\ s)\models
v(k)\geq \operatorname{maxCommittedVersion}(s,k)
$$

for a successful session-consistent read. A partially replicated region unable to satisfy the lower bound must not claim success under this contract.

**Related:** [Versioned Cache Races](../03-cache-and-partitioning/cache-invalidation-race.qmd), [Data Consistency](../../data-consistency.qmd).
